blocks.learningGoal: Distinguish atom economy from percentage yield and identify the desired product.

content.centralQuestion: How much of the reactant mass becomes the product we actually want?
content.keyDistinction: Yield compares actual with theoretical product; atom economy compares desired product with all products/reactants in the balanced equation.
objectives: Identify the desired product and by-products in a balanced equation.
Explain atom economy as the proportion of reactant atoms ending in the desired product.
Calculate percentage atom economy using coefficient × Mr values.
Explain why high atom economy supports sustainable and economic manufacture.
Distinguish atom economy from percentage yield.
Evaluate reaction routes using several supplied criteria.

blocks.learningGoal: Explain atom economy as the proportion of reactant atoms ending in the desired product.

content.formula: percentage atom economy = total Mr of desired product / total Mr of all reactants × 100
content.explanation: Atoms are conserved, but a reaction may make more than one product. Atom economy measures what fraction of the starting-material mass is built into the product we want rather than into by-products.
rules: Multiply each Mr by its coefficient.
Include every reactant in the denominator.
Atom economy is theoretical and cannot be improved by more careful laboratory technique.

blocks.learningGoal: Track conserved reactant mass into desired product and by-products.

content.representation: premium realistic lime-kiln mass-allocation figure with real-text calculation equivalent
content.assessedInformation: reactant total = desired product mass + by-product mass
content.example: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2; 100 mass units -> 56 desired + 44 by-product

blocks.learningGoal: Explore how changing the desired product changes atom economy without changing the balanced reaction.

accessibility.label: Atom allocation explorer
accessibility.description: Compare the fraction of calcium carbonate mass forming calcium oxide with the fraction forming carbon dioxide.
accessibility.keyboardInstructions: Use the product buttons to choose the desired product; the same values are presented in the fallback diagram and text.

blocks.learningGoal: Calculate atom economy for a one-to-one decomposition equation.
Use coefficients when calculating the total relative formula mass of reactants.
Evaluate reaction routes using atom economy alongside other supplied evidence.

content.guardrail: A higher atom economy alone does not automatically prove the best industrial route.
content.method: Compare every supplied criterion, identify trade-offs, then make a supported judgement.

blocks.learningGoal: Demonstrate secure calculation, interpretation and route-evaluation skills.

diagnostic.stem: What do coefficients in a balanced equation represent?
diagnostic.feedback: Coefficients give relative numbers of particles and moles.

diagnostic.stem: Which statement describes conservation of mass?
options: Total reactant mass equals total product mass
diagnostic.feedback: Atoms are rearranged, so total mass is conserved in a closed system.

diagnostic.stem: Which value is needed to calculate a compound's Mr?
diagnostic.feedback: Add the relative atomic masses shown by the formula.

guided.stem: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. CaO is desired. Calculate the atom economy. Mr: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56.
hints: Desired product goes in the numerator.

guided.stem: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Water is desired. Calculate the atom economy.
TiO2 + 2Mg -> Ti + 2MgO. Titanium is desired. Calculate the atom economy. Mr: TiO2 = 80; Mg = 24; Ti = 48.

independent.stem: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. If CO2 is the desired product, what is the atom economy? Mr: CaCO3 = 100; CO2 = 44.
independent.feedback: 44 / 100 × 100 = 44%. Changing the desired product changes the numerator.

independent.stem: Which reaction has 100% atom economy for its only product?
independent.feedback: Water is the only product, so every reactant atom enters the desired product.

independent.stem: Why must a coefficient multiply Mr in an atom-economy calculation?
options: It gives the number of formula units in the equation
independent.feedback: Coefficient × Mr gives that substance's relative mass contribution.

independent.stem: A reaction has 70% atom economy but 90% yield. What do the values mean?
options: 70% of reactant mass is in desired product; 90% of theoretical desired product was obtained
independent.feedback: Atom economy measures allocation; yield measures practical recovery.

independent.stem: Which change can improve percentage yield but cannot change atom economy for a fixed equation?
independent.feedback: Careful transfer may improve recovery, but the equation fixes atom economy.

examPractice.stem: State what is meant by atom economy.
markScheme: The percentage/proportion of reactant atoms or mass that forms the desired product.

examPractice.stem: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Calculate the atom economy for CaO. Mr: CaCO3 = 100; CaO = 56.
Explain why a reaction with high atom economy can support sustainable manufacture.
markScheme: More reactant atoms enter the desired product
Less waste/by-product is produced or fewer resources are wasted

examPractice.stem: Cu2S + O2 -> 2Cu + SO2. Calculate the atom economy for SO2. Mr: Cu2S = 159; O2 = 32; SO2 = 64. Give 2 significant figures.
A student says that improving filtration will increase atom economy. Explain why this is incorrect.
markScheme: Filtration may improve actual recovery/percentage yield
Atom economy is calculated from the balanced equation
The equation and allocation to desired/by-products are unchanged

examPractice.stem: Route A has 82% atom economy, 65% yield and a fast rate. Route B has 68% atom economy, 92% yield, a slower rate and a useful by-product. Evaluate which route should be chosen.
markScheme: Route A creates less waste by atom economy
Route B recovers more theoretical product
Route B's by-product may have value/reduce effective waste
Supported judgement acknowledging that more cost/energy/equilibrium data may be needed

exit.stem: Which quantity is fixed by a balanced equation?
exit.feedback: Atom economy follows the equation's allocation of atoms.

exit.stem: Desired Mr = 72 and total reactant Mr = 120. What is the atom economy?
